strengths: Originality: The observation-conditioned pruner, global computation-budget objective, and cross-timestep/cross-block cache reuse form a coherent and reasonably novel approach to diffusion-policy acceleration.

Significance: Reducing diffusion-policy latency is practically important for robotic control, and the reported 3.4–4.0× simulation speedups at roughly 91% pruning would be useful if independently substantiated.

Soundness: The evaluation spans RoboMimic PH/MH tasks, Franka Kitchen, several acceleration baselines, component ablations, and one physical-robot task. The policy is kept frozen, helping isolate the effect of the added pruner and reuse mechanism.

Presentation: The high-level prune-then-reuse pipeline and pseudocode are understandable. The paper reports hardware, core training hyperparameters, pretrained-checkpoint sources, latency, and variability for the principal simulation tables.
The ablations indicate that observation-dependent pruning, global budget allocation, and one-for-all reuse each matter, with especially large degradation from replacing the global sparsity loss.
weaknesses: Soundness: Several reported results are internally inconsistent. The SAG success rates in Table 4 differ substantially from Tables 1–2 for ostensibly the same tasks—for example, MH Transport is 62% versus 50%, and PH Square is 94% versus 89%—without any explanation of different checkpoints, seeds, or protocols. This undermines confidence in the central empirical evidence.

The captions' claimed average performance gains of 13% and 29% are undefined and do not match comparison with full precision: SAG averages about 84.4% versus 83.2% on PH and exactly 80.75% versus 80.75% on MH. Several individual SAG results are also below full precision, so repeated claims of universally “lossless” acceleration are overstated.

The evidence motivating rollout adaptivity is weak. Figure 1 considers only three randomly generated schedules and intervenes at one rollout iteration at a time, yet the paper infers that the “optimal” schedule changes. This neither searches for an optimum nor establishes that observation conditioning is necessary. The fixed-schedule ablation also does not explain how its single schedule is constructed.

The comparison does not establish a robust performance–efficiency frontier. Most methods are evaluated at one author-selected operating point rather than matched latency, FLOPs, or success rate; no sweep over SAG pruning rates is reported for task success. At comparable speed, improvements over DDIM or BAC are often small or within the reported variability.

The physical-robot evidence is insufficient for the paper's real-time-control claims: it covers one simple task, omits the number of evaluation trials, uncertainty, seeds, and failure analysis, and reports an unexpectedly low 3% success for the unaccelerated policy versus 54% for SAG. Because the pruner receives additional supervised training, this large reversal requires careful explanation and controlled replication.

The statistical protocol is underspecified. “Three fixed seeds” is inadequate without the number of evaluation episodes per seed and the meaning of the ± values, and no significance or confidence analysis is provided. Hyperparameter-selection and validation/test separation are also unclear.

Methodological details needed to evaluate or reproduce the method are missing: pruner dimensions and parameter count, observation encoder specification and initialization, timestep/block grouping, the norm used in the fidelity loss, handling of diffusion randomness during direct action supervision, exact STE implementation, and whether separate pruners are trained for every task. Equation 10 also alternates between describing the mask as binary and as a continuous learned gate.

The cross-block reuse justification is incomplete. High cosine similarity alone does not establish that residual outputs from different layer depths are safely interchangeable, and Appendix A.7 lacks quantitative summaries, task/sample details, or an intervention relating similarity to action error and success.

Presentation and benchmark descriptions contain material errors. RoboMimic Square is a square-nut placement task, not tracing a square path as stated in Figure 1 and Appendix A.2. The real-world text reports “45.1%” inference frequency while Figure 5 shows 40.5 Hz, and Appendix A.5 states the speedup ratio in the inverse direction. Its displayed average latencies also do not equal the averages of the listed task columns.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance: the project-page field is blank, no code or trained pruners are supplied, and baseline adaptations are described only briefly. Providing source checkpoints and several optimizer settings is helpful but insufficient to reproduce the reported schedules and results.

Limitations and ethics are not treated adequately. There is no limitations discussion addressing task-specific training, distribution shift, hardware dependence, or the possibility that cached activations cause unsafe actions. Given the low real-robot success rates, deployment safeguards and failure consequences should be discussed. Overall, the promising idea is outweighed by unresolved evidential inconsistencies and reproducibility gaps.

strengths: Originality/significance: Observation-conditioned, rollout-adaptive pruning is a sensible extension of static diffusion-policy caching, and sharing cached activations across blocks as well as timesteps is an interesting design direction.

Evaluation breadth: The paper compares against several acceleration approaches on RoboMimic PH/MH tasks, Kitchen, and a real-robot pick-and-release task; it also reports component ablations and wall-clock latency rather than FLOPs alone.
Presentation: The high-level prune-then-reuse pipeline is understandable, and the main algorithm, pruning objective, hardware, training set sizes, and key hyperparameters are provided.
The reported results, if validated, would be practically useful: SAG generally retains baseline simulation success while producing roughly 3.4–4.0x reported speedups.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central evidence for rollout adaptivity is weak. Figure 1 evaluates only three randomly generated schedules using an unclear leave-one-out protocol, yet the text calls different schedules “optimal.” This neither characterizes the schedule space nor demonstrates that observation conditioning discovers causally appropriate schedules. The fixed-schedule ablation is also underspecified and improves average success by only about six points on the selected grouping.

Reported numbers contain serious unexplained inconsistencies. SAG's main-table results differ substantially from its ablation-table results for ostensibly identical settings—for example, Square-MH is 79% in Table 2 but 86% in Table 4, and Transport-MH is 50% versus 62%. The real-world text states 45.1% inference frequency, whereas Figure 5 shows 40.5 Hz. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the evaluation.

The latency evidence is internally inconsistent. Table 5 reports SDP latency of 1.92 s on Square while Tables 1–2 claim about 1.70x speedup; relative to the 1.56 s full model, this is approximately 0.81x. Several “Average” latency entries also do not equal the averages of the displayed task columns, and the stated speedup formula is inverted. Timing methodology lacks synchronization, warm-up, repetition, variance, and batch-size details.

The paper repeatedly calls the method “real-time,” but simulation latency is approximately 0.42–0.47 s per generation, while the real-robot result is 40.5 Hz—below the paper's own claimed 50 Hz lower requirement for Franka control. The relationship among action-chunk generation rate, execution/control rate, and closed-loop responsiveness is not analyzed.

Statistical support is inadequate. The manuscript mentions three seeds but does not state the number of evaluation rollouts, define what the ± values represent, provide confidence intervals or significance tests, or report real-robot trial counts and uncertainty. Consequently, small claimed gains over full precision or BAC cannot be distinguished from evaluation noise.

Methodological details are ambiguous. The “fidelity” objective is described as matching an output distribution but is written as an unspecified norm between a stochastic diffusion-policy output and one expert action. The treatment of diffusion noise during training, norm/reduction, STE implementation, observation encoder architecture, cache tensor compatibility across layers, and behavior when an early pruned block reads the zero-initialized global cache are not adequately specified.

The one-for-all ablation shows an empirical success difference but does not support the paper's assertion that it “reduces redundancy”; no cache-error or approximation-error comparison is reported. Likewise, cosine similarity between activations does not by itself show that substituting one block's residual for another is safe.

Significance/generalization is overstated. Experiments use one DP-T architecture and appear to train a separate pruner on thousands of samples for every task. There is no cross-task transfer, distribution-shift test, comparison across policy sizes, or evaluation on the VLA models emphasized in the introduction. Thus the evidence supports task-specific compression more than a broadly applicable acceleration method.

Reproducibility is insufficient for reliable reconstruction. The project-page field is blank, no code is supplied, and important evaluation and baseline-adaptation details are missing. Baseline hyperparameters are largely single chosen configurations, with no matched speed/compute trade-off curves to establish superiority at comparable budgets.

Presentation includes overclaims and numerical ambiguity: “lossless” is used despite several lower success rates, “without updating model parameters” obscures that a new pruner is trained, and the claimed 13%/29% average performance gains in table captions have no clear reference and do not match gains over full precision.

Limitations and ethics: There is no substantive limitations section discussing task-specific training, failure modes of erroneous cache reuse, distribution shift, hardware dependence, or reduced safety margins in closed-loop robotic control. No material ethical violation is evident, but deployment and robot-safety considerations are omitted. Overall, the promising idea is outweighed by inconsistent measurements and insufficient evidence for the central adaptivity, real-time, and lossless claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck: diffusion-policy latency in closed-loop robotic control. The observation-conditioned pruning schedule is a plausible and useful extension beyond static caching.

The combination of a real-time pruner, global sparsity objective, and cross-timestep/cross-block activation reuse is technically interesting. Component ablations in Table 4 show substantial degradation when each major design is removed.

The empirical scope is comparatively broad: RoboMimic PH/MH tasks, the multi-stage Kitchen benchmark, several acceleration baselines, wall-clock latency measurements, and a real-robot pick-and-release experiment. SAG generally preserves the full policy's success rate while obtaining approximately 3.4–4.0× speedup.

Presentation is visually polished and the high-level pipeline is easy to follow. The paper also discloses its limited use of language models. No major ethical concern is apparent from the reported study. weaknesses: The evidence does not cleanly establish the central claim that rollout-adaptive pruning is superior to static scheduling. Figure 1 uses only three randomly generated schedules, while the main ablation replaces the adaptive pruner with an insufficiently specified fixed schedule. Stronger controls should include an optimized static schedule, observation-independent learned pruner, and matched-compute comparisons across pruning rates.

The headline advantage is overstated. DDIM already provides roughly 3.3× speedup with near-baseline success, so SAG's gain is often only about 10–20% additional throughput. On MH tasks, SAG and SDP have the same average success despite very different speed. The captions' claimed average performance gains of 13% and 29% are not explained and do not follow directly from the tabulated averages.

Statistical reporting is inadequate. The paper mentions three fixed seeds but does not state the number of evaluation rollouts, what the ± values represent, or whether differences are statistically significant. The real-robot result reports neither trial counts nor uncertainty, making the apparent improvement from 38% to 54% difficult to assess.

Reproducibility is materially incomplete: the project-page field is blank, no code is supplied, and important pruner specifications are absent, including encoder architecture, transformer depth/width/heads, MLP dimensions, mask-temperature or STE details, convergence criteria, training time, and exact latency-measurement protocol. The claimed 0.3% overhead is not substantiated by a component-level latency breakdown.

Several technical definitions are ambiguous. Equations 8–9 appear to nest expectations inconsistently and compare a stochastic generated action directly with one demonstrated action without explaining noise control or the precise norm. The mask is defined as binary but later treated as a continuous gating value. The text says the cache is shared among blocks of the same type, whereas Algorithm 2 initializes one global cache, leaving the implemented reuse semantics unclear.

There are notable internal inconsistencies: SAG results differ between Tables 1–2 and Table 4 without explanation; Figure 5 reports 40.5 Hz while the text states 45.1%; and the paper calls the method parameter-update-free even though a task-specific pruner is trained using thousands of samples. These issues weaken confidence in the experimental account.

The limitations discussion is effectively absent. Important limitations include task-specific training and demonstration access, evaluation on only one policy architecture, limited hardware coverage, possible distribution-shift sensitivity of observation-conditioned masks, and safety/failure behavior when aggressive pruning is deployed on a physical robot. Overall, the idea is promising, but the evidential and reproducibility gaps warrant substantial revision before reliable acceptance.

strengths: Originality: The observation-conditioned, rollout-adaptive pruning formulation is a useful departure from fixed diffusion-caching schedules. Globally allocating computation over denoising steps and transformer blocks, together with cross-block reuse, is a plausible and interesting contribution.

Significance: Accelerating diffusion policies is important for closed-loop robotics. The reported 3.4–4.0× simulation speedups and roughly 44–46 Hz real-robot inference would be practically meaningful if validated under a fully specified protocol.

Soundness: The evaluation covers five RoboMimic tasks, Kitchen, three real-robot tasks, several caching/distillation baselines, wall-clock latency, pruning-rate sensitivity, component ablations, sampler compatibility, and observation perturbations. Results generally indicate a favorable success/latency trade-off.

Presentation: The main pipeline is organized clearly, and the figures, equations, and tables are visually legible. The paper also candidly notes limits concerning policy families, platforms, task diversity, fixed compute budgets, and reliance on reference data.
weaknesses: Soundness: The evidence for the central rollout-adaptivity claim is inadequate. Figure 1 uses only three randomly generated schedules, applies each at one rollout iteration, and reports no uncertainty or controlled comparison against an optimized static schedule. The decisive fixed-pruner ablation is insufficiently specified, so it is unclear whether its six-point average gap represents adaptivity or a weak static baseline.

Soundness: Reported results are internally inconsistent. The complete SAG row in Table 6 differs materially from Tables 1–3 on many tasks—for example Square-PH is 94 versus 89, Transport-MH is 62 versus 50, and Can-PH is 94 versus 98—without explaining different runs or protocols. Table 9's stated averages also do not equal the means of its displayed task columns. These discrepancies undermine the quantitative conclusions.

Methodological specification is incomplete and sometimes contradictory. The text says there is a shared cache for blocks of the same type, implying separate SA, CA, and FFN caches, whereas Equations 12–13 and Algorithm 2 use one global buffer. The fidelity-loss norm, handling of diffusion randomness, exact straight-through estimator, mask initialization, pruner dimensions/parameter count, observation encoder, and task-specific versus shared training are not fully defined.

The paper equates the fraction of gated sub-blocks with the fraction of pruned computation even though self-attention, cross-attention, and FFN have different costs. There is no FLOP, memory, or latency breakdown showing pruner overhead, and the timing protocol omits synchronization, warm-up, batch size, and variance. Thus the wall-clock speedups are promising but not independently interpretable.

Experimental statistics are insufficient. The manuscript mentions three fixed seeds but does not clearly state rollout counts, whether deviations are across checkpoints or evaluation seeds, or significance tests. Real-robot percentages have no trial counts or uncertainty in the main experiment. Claims of 13% and 29% average performance gains are not defined and do not describe gains over full computation, which are small or absent on average.

Reproducibility is weak: the project-page field is blank, no code or trained pruners are supplied, and key dataset splits, reference-sample construction, baseline tuning, real-robot policy training, action horizons, control protocol, and complete architecture details are missing. Others could not reliably reproduce the method or its comparisons from the manuscript.

Presentation contains credibility-relevant errors. RoboMimic Square is described as tracing a square path rather than inserting a square nut onto a peg, some claims overinterpret changing masks as proof of useful adaptation, and the references contain placeholders such as “Placeholder Publisher” and “Submitted to Some Conference.”

The impact statement is inaccurate and incomplete: it says all experiments use public simulation datasets and no new human involvement, despite reporting newly collected teleoperation demonstrations and real-robot experiments. It also dismisses ethical risk without discussing operator consent, robot safety procedures, or failure risks from dynamically skipping control-policy computation. These concerns are remediable but should be addressed.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical bottleneck: diffusion-policy latency in closed-loop robotic control. Observation-conditioned pruning combined with cross-timestep and cross-block activation reuse is a sensible, potentially useful direction.

The empirical scope is comparatively broad, covering nine RoboMimic variants, Franka Kitchen, three real-robot tasks, multiple acceleration baselines, pruning-rate sensitivity, component ablations, sampler compatibility, and observation perturbations.

The reported efficiency results are promising: approximately 3.4–4.0× simulation speedups and 44–46 Hz action generation on the real robot, generally without reducing the headline aggregate success rates relative to full computation.

The method freezes the underlying policy and trains the pruner from a relatively small reference set, which could make the approach more practical than policy distillation. The paper also acknowledges limitations involving policy families, hardware, task diversity, reference data, and fixed compute budgets.
weaknesses: Soundness is undermined by major unexplained inconsistencies across results. For example, the main tables report SAG success rates of 98/89/85/50 on Can/Square/Transport/Tool PH and 94/79/50 on Can/Square/Transport MH, whereas Table 6 reports 94/94/84/54 and 96/86/62, respectively. Figures 3 and 13 also give different sinusoidal-encoding results for ostensibly the same tasks. The manuscript does not identify different protocols, checkpoints, or sample sizes that would explain these discrepancies.

Several prominent quantitative claims are unsupported or misleading. The captions claim average performance gains of 13% on PH and 29% on MH, but SAG improves over full computation by only about 1.2 percentage points on PH and is essentially tied on MH. If the claimed gains use another comparator or definition, it is never specified. Likewise, Table 9 lists a full-computation average latency of 1.66 s although its five entries average about 1.56 s, and the stated description of the speedup ratio is reversed.

The central evidence for rollout adaptivity is weak. Figure 1 tests only three randomly generated schedules in a leave-one-out intervention, without confidence intervals, schedule construction details, or statistical tests. Variation among random schedules at individual rollout positions does not establish that an observation-conditioned schedule is necessary or optimal. The ablation replaces the adaptive pruner with an insufficiently described fixed schedule and does not compare against strong matched alternatives such as rollout-index-conditioned pruning, optimized per-task schedules, or randomized masks.

Evaluation uncertainty is inadequately documented. The number of simulation episodes is omitted, “three fixed seeds” is ambiguous, and it is unclear whether reported deviations are across training seeds, evaluation seeds, or episodes. Real-robot success percentages have no trial counts, uncertainty intervals, paired conditions, or significance analysis. Consequently, improvements such as 26% to 58% on Assembly Line and several gains over the stochastic full policy cannot be assessed reliably.

The efficiency comparison is not fully controlled. Methods use different samplers and training procedures, while the latency protocol lacks warm-up, batch size, synchronization, repeated-run variability, memory usage, and an explicit accounting of pruner/observation-encoder cost. Reported frequency appears to measure action generation rather than end-to-end sensing and control, so it does not substantiate the broader real-time-control claim. The method reaches only about 44–46 Hz despite motivating the work with a 50–1000 Hz requirement.

The proposed reuse operation is technically ambiguous. The prose describes one buffer for blocks “of the same type,” while Algorithm 2 initializes one global buffer and updates it across every block, apparently mixing self-attention, cross-attention, and FFN outputs. Equations 12–13 do not resolve buffer indexing, initialization effects, tensor compatibility, or how reuse across architecturally distinct blocks remains meaningful. The similarity plots alone do not demonstrate that high cosine similarity makes such substitution safe.

Reproducibility is poor. The project-page field is blank, no code is supplied, and essential details are missing: observation-encoder architecture or initialization, pruner Transformer dimensions and depth, parameter/FLOP counts, precise mask grouping, diffusion settings, reference-set construction, loss norm and normalization, training randomness, evaluation episode counts, and baseline implementation details. The appendix claims to provide network architecture details but largely supplies only optimizer hyperparameters.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the work combines learned conditional gating, global sparsity regularization, and activation caching, all established ideas. Cross-block shared reuse is the most distinctive element, but it is insufficiently specified and validated. There is no controlled decomposition separating the benefit of conditioning on observations from rollout position, task identity, regularization, or the shared-cache mechanism.

Presentation is polished visually but overstates conclusions. Statements such as “superior,” “without sacrificing performance,” and “robustness and reliability” are not justified by the uncertainty analysis. Some descriptions of benchmark tasks appear inaccurate, the bibliography contains placeholders such as “Placeholder Publisher” and “Submitted to Some Conference,” and notation alternates between binary and continuous masks without a precise training-time definition.

The limitations and ethics discussions are incomplete. The paper does not discuss per-task pruner training, distribution-shift sensitivity, catastrophic degradation at 97% pruning, physical-robot safety implications, or the lack of end-to-end latency evidence. The impact statement says no new human-involved data were collected, yet the experiments report collecting 200 teleoperated demonstrations per real-world task; this apparent contradiction should be clarified. strengths: Originality: SAG combines observation-conditioned, rollout-adaptive pruning with shared cross-timestep and cross-block activation reuse. This is a meaningful extension beyond static diffusion-policy caching schedules.

Soundness: The evaluation is broad, covering ten simulation settings, pruning-rate sensitivity, component ablations, sampler compatibility, visual perturbations, and three real-robot tasks. Reported wall-clock results show roughly 3.4–4.0× speedups while generally preserving baseline success rates.

Significance: Reducing diffusion-policy latency is practically important. The real-robot results demonstrate frequencies around 44–46 Hz versus 7 Hz for full computation, including an improvement from 26% to 58% success on the Assembly Line task.

Presentation: The motivation, three-level redundancy formulation, prune-then-reuse pipeline, and algorithms are generally clear. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges restricted policy families, platforms, tasks, fixed compute budgets, and dependence on reference data.

The global sparsity, adaptive-pruner, and one-for-all reuse ablations suggest that each proposed component contributes materially. The compute-matched comparison with Consistency Policy also supports sparse within-step computation over aggressively shortening diffusion trajectories.
Research ethics: The work appears low risk and includes an impact statement; no material privacy, discrimination, or dual-use concern is apparent for the studied manipulation tasks.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central evidence for rollout adaptivity is not sufficiently controlled. Figure 1 uses only three randomly generated schedules, while the fixed-schedule ablation does not explain how its schedule is constructed or optimized. Consequently, it does not establish that observation-conditioned adaptation outperforms a strong compute-matched static schedule.

Soundness: Simulation reporting is internally inconsistent. SAG results in the main tables differ substantially from the ablation table—for example, PH Can/Square/Tool are 98/89/50 in Table 1 but 94/94/54 in Table 6, and MH Square/Transport are 79/50 in Table 2 but 86/62 in Table 6. Figure 3 also conflicts with Table 6 and Figure 13. The manuscript does not explain whether these use different runs, checkpoints, or evaluation protocols.

Evaluation rigor: The number of evaluation episodes, meaning of the reported error bars, seed aggregation procedure, checkpoint selection, and statistical significance are not specified. Real-robot results provide neither trial counts nor uncertainty, making the striking Assembly Line improvement difficult to assess.

Significance: DDIM already obtains about 3.3× speedup with mostly comparable performance, so SAG's incremental latency advantage is modest on several tasks. Although DPM-Solver compatibility is tested, latency for DPM50+SAG is omitted, preventing verification of the claimed complementary acceleration benefit.

Reproducibility: Important implementation details are missing, including pruner dimensions and parameter count, observation encoder specification, precise fidelity-loss norm and stochastic-noise handling, cache-buffer semantics, baseline implementation details, and training cost. The project-page field is empty and no code is provided.

Presentation: Claims such as average performance gains of 13% and 29% do not identify the comparison baseline and are not supported relative to full computation or the strongest baseline. The text also states that speedup is computed as accelerated time divided by original time, which is the inverse of the reported convention.

Method description: The prose says that a shared cache is maintained for blocks of the same type, whereas Algorithm 2 initializes one global cache and appears to reuse it across all block types. This ambiguity is consequential because self-attention, cross-attention, and FFN residuals have different semantics.

Limitations and ethics: The impact statement says all experiments use publicly available simulation data and no new human involvement, yet the paper reports newly collected teleoperation demonstrations for real-robot tasks. Physical-robot safety and the provenance/consent status of those demonstrations deserve brief clarification.
